en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.

At that time, the upāsaka Nandi together with five hundred upāsakas departed from the city of Rājagṛha, ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and approached the place where the Buddha was. They bowed their heads at his feet in salutation, knelt with palms joined, and asked the Buddha:
"O Great Virtuous One!..."
"I wish to hear about the five precepts of an upāsaka;
what evil consequences arise from violating the true precepts?
The Buddha replied:
“Nandi, lay follower!
There are ten evils in the taking of life.
What are these ten?
In this present life, one constantly harbors a harmful mind;
in future lives, that poisonous mind will flourish and blaze, leading to constant suffering and injury.
With resentment never ceasing, others take no pleasure in seeing such a person.
Their thoughts are full of evil, causing those who see them to feel dread;
they sleep uneasily,
and in their dreams they are filled with terror.
Upon awakening, one is struck with terror;
at the time of death, one becomes frantic and violent, planting the seeds for a short life;
and when the body breaks up and life ends, one is reborn in hell.
If one becomes a human being, one will have many illnesses and a short lifespan;
these are the ten evil consequences.
To steal or plunder the wealth of others has ten evil consequences.
What are the ten?
Their greed and gluttony are profound and heavy, and they are constantly beset by manifold doubts;
they are capable of giving rise to grave evils, acting at improper times and moving according to what is not the Dharma.
Relatives and friends act with hostility and rebellion, while the virtuous and good are kept at a distance;
they violate their precepts yet are bold and reckless;
they constantly fear royal surveillance and must seek wealth to purchase their lives.
They hoard various precious objects;
they engage in the occupation of poverty;
and when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.

Even if one should obtain human birth, one will suffer from hunger, cold, and hardship; it is extremely difficult to acquire wealth, and even if a small amount is obtained, it must be shared with five parties—the king, thieves, water, fire, and wicked wives and children.
Even if it is now buried away, it will inevitably be lost in the end.
These are the ten unwholesome deeds.
"There are ten unwholesome consequences of sexual misconduct.
What are these ten?
She constantly subjects her husband to surveillance, capture, and cruel torment, causing discord within the household;
wholesome dharmas are exhausted and extinguished while unwholesome dharmas increase;
she brings ruin and destruction upon her own body.
He does not restrain his wife nor guard his wealth;
he is constantly suspected by others and distrusted by his kinsmen;
such are the fruits of his karma.
Her conduct will not be chaste;
at the dissolution of the body after death, she will be reborn in hell;
and even if she should obtain birth as a woman, she will not have but a single husband.
Even if one obtains male birth, one will pursue illicit lust and lose one’s own wife;
these are the ten evil consequences of lying.
Within the act of false speech, there are ten evil consequences.
What are the ten?
Their mouths are constantly foul-smelling and putrid;
benevolent deities turn their backs on them, while malevolent ghosts easily assail them.
When one’s truthful words circulate through the world, they are not believed by the masses;
when worldly matters are treated as weighty, they do not enter into formal discourse.
Without any factual basis, an evil reputation spreads far and wide, leading others to despise and disparage one, such that no reverence or solemnity arises.
Although they speak the truth, people do not accept or practice it;
they harbor much sorrow and fear;
and they plant the karma of slander.
Upon the death of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in hell;
even if one should obtain human form, one will constantly be subjected to slander.
These are the ten evil deeds.
“There are thirty-five evils of drinking alcohol.
What are these thirty-five? They are:
squandering one’s wealth and property;”
It brings about manifold sufferings and afflictions;
it increases enmity and strife;
and it leaves the body exposed and naked.
Ill repute spreads far and wide;
the light of wisdom diminishes day by day;
that which should be attained is not obtained.
What has already been attained is lost;
it brings to light evil deeds;
and it suddenly gives rise to the root of anxiety and grief regarding essential matters.
They become dazed and vanish;
their countenances turn base and ugly;
they treat their elders and superiors with contempt.
They do not know how to make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
within their own households, they do not distinguish between the honorable and the lowly;
and they do not revere the Buddha.
They do not revere the Great Dharma;
they do not respectfully serve the Sangha;
instead, they are intimate with evil people.
They distance themselves from the power of clarity;
they fall away from the right path;
and they lack a sense of shame and remorse.
Not guarding the sense faculties;
being muddled by lustful desire;
and being unloved by the multitude.
People take no pleasure in seeing him;
virtuous elders all come to reproach him;
he accumulates a multitude of evils.
When employing their power, they do not anticipate the capacity of their task;
their wisdom and virtue remain concealed;
and they do not distinguish between similar types.
They are far removed from Nirvana;
they plant the karma of delusion and confusion;
when their bodies die and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.
"Even if they should obtain human birth, they will be foolish, dull-witted, and deaf.

At that time, the lay follower Nandi, the five hundred faithful laymen, the devas, the people of the world, and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, vowed to uphold it for the rest of their lives. They bowed their heads to the ground, circumambulated him, and departed with great joy.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home Spoken by the Buddha
